                            Atmospheric dynamics
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Climate and Earth system modelling
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Projection and prediction

MainSubseasonal forecasts—weather predictions 2–6 weeks ahead—lie at the heart of agricultural planning, water allocation, disaster preparedness and energy management1,2,3. Yet accurate prediction at this timescale remains difficult. Today, our best estimates of future weather come from dynamical models that numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans change over time4,5 and artificial intelligence (AI) models that learn to predict the weather from historical data6,7,8. Because of the steady improvements in modelling, computation and data collection over the past half-century, deterministic forecasting systems can now provide accurate point estimates of the weather 1–2 weeks in advance10. However, the 2-week horizon also marks a transition in predictability: beyond this point, even small differences in initial weather conditions can lead to dramatic differences in outcomes and a single deterministic forecast cannot capture this uncertainty20.To surmount this predictability barrier, one often turns to probabilistic forecasting, that is, predicting a distribution over future weather rather than a single point estimate21,22,23. Probabilistic forecasting explicitly encodes forecast uncertainty and provides actionable estimates of the likelihood of high-impact extreme events. For both dynamical and AI models, probabilistic forecasts are typically generated by perturbing the inputs, parameters or internal state of a model to produce an ensemble of possible future weather states13,23,24,25. Although these ensembles are routinely skilful at shorter lead times (to 15 days), operational dynamical ensembles and even state-of-the-art probabilistic AI routinely underperform the climatological average at longer subseasonal lead times, especially outside the tropics13.A core difficulty is that leading subseasonal ensembles are generated iteratively over many time steps and even small per-step modelling errors compound into large systematic errors over several weeks14. This effect is especially pronounced for precipitation, which is sensitive to cascading inaccuracies across model components and highly variable in space and time4,26. Indeed, subseasonal forecasting has long been considered a ‘predictability desert’ because of the compounding model errors and complex interdependencies among the atmosphere, land, ocean and sea-ice components that evolve with different timescales11,15.Although existing subseasonal ensembles are indeed error-prone, we show that a component of their systematic error is predictable and correctable using machine learning, allowing significant gains in skill with minimal cost. To achieve this, we introduce a probabilistic bias correction (PBC) framework that adaptively learns to correct the forecast distribution of a model using its own historical predictions and observations of past weather. PBC is compatible with any input model and we use it to advance the state of the art in both data-driven and hybrid (AI + dynamical) subseasonal forecasting. The resulting forecasts are designed for operational deployment and, in real-time competition18, outperform the best alternative dynamical, AI and hybrid forecasting systems from forecasting centres and competitors around the globe.Probabilistic bias correctionPBC is a new machine learning framework for improving subseasonal forecasts from dynamical, AI or hybrid prediction systems. Given a raw ensemble of deterministic forecasts, PBC outputs learning-enhanced probabilities designed to correct systematic errors while preserving the predictive signal in the underlying model. Our approach is inspired by the deterministic bias correction framework of ref. 27 but operates directly on the space of probability distributions rather than at the level of raw observations. The added flexibility allows us to directly optimize not only the centre of a distribution but also its spread and shape.Figure 1 illustrates a sample application of PBC. First, an input ensemble is converted into an initial probabilistic forecast compared with climatological quantile bins derived from historical observations or from the hindcasts of the model. Next, two computationally efficient machine learning models—Debias++ and Persistence++—are applied in parallel to produce complementary corrections of the initial forecast. Debias++ perturbs the forecast using location-, date- and quantile-specific corrections learned by minimizing probabilistic forecasting error over adaptively selected training periods. Meanwhile, Persistence++ blends the forecast with lagged observations and climatology to account for recent weather trends and day-of-year effects. Finally, the two corrections are projected onto the space of valid cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) and averaged to form the final PBC prediction. The Methods provide further details.Fig. 1: PBC schematic.Full size imagePBC takes as input lagged observations, climatological quantiles (for example, quintiles, terciles or deciles) and the deterministic forecasts of any dynamical or AI model and outputs a learning-enhanced probabilistic forecast designed to correct systematic prediction errors. Coastlines from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com/).This framework can be used to improve forecasts for any weather variable, any spatial grid and any number of quantile bins. For concreteness, we adopt the following conventions of the AI Weather Quest subseasonal forecasting competition18 run by the ECMWF. First, we focus on forecasting average 2-m temperature (over land), total precipitation (over land) and average mean sea-level pressure on a global 1.5° latitude–longitude grid with five quintile bins. Second, we evaluate subseasonal forecasts for week 3 (days 19–25) and week 4 (days 26–32) using ranked probability skill score (RPSS)28, a standard measure of forecast improvement compared with a climatological baseline. Further details on the forecasting targets and evaluation are described in the Methods.To assess the operational utility and versatility of PBC, we apply the framework to three state-of-the-art subseasonal forecasting models: the industry-leading dynamical ensemble from ECMWF17, subseasonal AI Forecasting System (AIFS-SUBS) from ECMWF16 and post-processing ensembles with transformers (POET), a hybrid model that postprocesses the ECMWF dynamical ensemble with convolutional and transformer neural networks29. As our measure of ground truth, we adopt the ERA5 reanalysis dataset30, which assimilates a wide range of observations to produce a global gridded record of the Earth’s weather from 1940 to the present, but any other target for correction could be substituted. Because PBC is so lightweight, we also incrementally retrain it each day, using only the reanalysis and model forecast data that would have been observable on each forecast issuance date to mimic operational deployment (Methods).Correcting dynamical forecasts with PBCFigure 2 summarizes the pronounced skill gains obtained when PBC is applied to the dynamical ensemble from ECMWF, widely considered to be the most accurate weather model in the world and the gold standard for benchmarking subseasonal skill31,32. For each target variable and lead time, Fig. 2a reports global RPSS over the years 2016–2024, whereas Fig. 2b shows the spatial RPSS distribution over the same time period. Negative RPSS indicates worse predictive performance than the climatological baseline, whereas positive RPSS indicates improved performance. PBC consistently improves the low-scoring raw ECMWF ensemble, tripling its positive precipitation skill (0.023 RPSS) and converting its negative-skill temperature and mean sea-level pressure forecasts into skilful predictions that consistently outperform climatology (Fig. 2a). Analogous gains are observed when skill is stratified by season (Extended Data Fig. 1) or by region (Extended Data Fig. 2) and the improvements are accompanied by a pronounced reduction in systematic model bias across the globe (Extended Data Figs. 3, 4 and 5).Fig. 2: Global forecast skill of ECMWF and its correction.Full size imagea, Across the years 2016–2024, PBC boosts the subseasonal skill of raw ECMWF forecasts more effectively than operational debiasing, transforming low- and no-skill inputs into skilful outputs that consistently outperform climatology. Negative RPSS indicates predictive performance worse than climatology, positive RPSS indicates improved performance and cross-hatching indicates significant improvement (paired one-sided stationary block bootstrap P < 0.05 for 239 target dates) compared with raw and debiased ECMWF. b, PBC improvements are broadly distributed with 98% of grid cells showing skill gains compared with debiased ECMWF for precipitation, 91–92% for temperature and 89–91% for sea-level pressure. Arid grid cells with no climatological precipitation are excluded. Coastlines in b from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com/).Source dataTo dampen the systemic effects of model bias, forecasting centres routinely debias their operational forecasts by comparing each deterministic prediction to quantiles derived from model hindcasts rather than observations33. Given the same deterministic predictions as input, PBC consistently outperforms this operational debiasing protocol, replacing the near-zero precipitation skill of debiased ECMWF with consistently positive RPSS and boosting the positive temperature and pressure RPSS of debiased ECMWF by 26–37% and 16–32% (above baseline skills of 0.07–0.10 and 0.06–0.11) respectively (Fig. 2a). The PBC gains compared with debiased ECMWF are also broadly distributed with 98% of grid cells showing skill gains for precipitation, 91–92% for temperature and 89–91% for sea-level pressure (Fig. 2b). These results demonstrate that PBC can transform unskilful inputs into reliably skilful outputs and serve as an improved drop-in replacement for existing operational debiasing protocols.In fact, PBC can boost the skill of its dynamical input beyond the levels of existing AI-based subseasonal models. For example, ref. 13 recently introduced FuXi-S2S, a deep learning model that outperforms the dynamical ensemble of ECMWF at subseasonal lead times. Across the globe and the test years 2017–2021, PBC-ECMWF shows a pronounced increase in skill compared with FuXi-S2S for each variable and lead time, with 99–100% of grid cells showing skill gains for temperature, 97–99% for precipitation and 96–100% for mean sea-level pressure (Extended Data Fig. 6).Decomposing PBC into its component parts (Extended Data Fig. 7a) yields four more insights into its skill gains. First, Debias++ and Persistence++ each significantly improve (P < 0.05) on raw ECMWF for all targets. Second, Persistence++ alone significantly improves (P < 0.05) on debiased ECMWF for each target except week-4 pressure, whereas Debias++ provides smaller improvements. Third, projection minimally affects skill as Debias++ and Persistence++ forecasts are typically valid CDFs. Finally, ensembling the complementary Persistence++ and Debias++ forecasts offers robust improvements across all variables and lead times.Correcting AI forecasts with PBCPBC can also be used to improve the skill of AI models. For example, Fig. 3a shows the substantial skill gains obtained when PBC is applied to the state-of-the-art subseasonal AIFS-SUBS of ECMWF. The AIFS is a deep learning model that exhibits greater subseasonal skill than debiased ECMWF for the challenging task of precipitation forecasting and comparable skill for temperature and mean sea-level pressure prediction16. Across the globe and the 2025 test year, PBC consistently amplifies AIFS-SUBS skill, doubling its mean RPSS (0.03) across all variables and lead times.Fig. 3: Global forecast skill of AI models and their corrections.Full size imagea, In 2025, PBC consistently enhances the subseasonal skill of ECMWF AIFS-SUBS, doubling its average skill (0.03) across all variables and lead times. b, In 2024, the hybrid (AI + dynamical) model POET already improves the skill of its dynamical input, ECMWF. Nevertheless, PBC further enhances skill for every variable and lead time with gains of 68–98% for precipitation (compared with baseline skills of 0.03–0.04), 15–23% for mean sea-level pressure (compared with baseline skills of 0.08–0.10) and 5–7% for temperature (compared with baseline skills of 0.16–0.19). Cross-hatching indicates significant improvement (paired one-sided stationary block bootstrap P < 0.05 for (a) 179 and (b) 104 week 3 and 107 week 4 target dates) compared with all baselines.Source dataWe also apply PBC to a hybrid (AI + dynamical) forecasting system, POET. POET takes as input a dynamical ensemble (in this case, ECMWF) and outputs a new ensemble with all members simultaneously corrected by a transformer embedded in a convolutional neural network29. POET serves as challenging input for PBC as its ensemble has already been corrected by AI and is substantially more skilful than its raw ECMWF input. Moreover, POET has been shown to outperform other statistical and AI-based post-processing techniques including member-by-member model output statistics34,35, ensemble model output statistics36, LeNet neural network post-processing37 and pure transformer-based post-processing38. Nevertheless, PBC enhances POET skill for every variable and lead time with RPSS gains of 68–98% for precipitation (compared with baseline skills of 0.03–0.04), 15–23% for mean sea-level pressure (compared with baseline skills of 0.08–0.10) and 5–7% for temperature (compared with baseline skills of 0.16–0.19) in 2024 (Fig. 3b).A decomposition of PBC into its component parts (Extended Data Fig. 7b) shows three distinct features contributing to its improvements. First, Debias++ alone improves on its POET input for each task, highlighting the value of direct CDF optimization compared with correction only in deterministic forecast space27,29,34,35,38. Second, Persistence++ delivers even greater skill for precipitation, highlighting the value of integrating recent observations compared with a correction that ignores this source of predictability29,34,35,36,38,39. Third, ensembling the two complementary corrections robustly captures the strengths of each, highlighting the value of model merging compared with monolithic correction29,34,35,36,37,38,39.AI Weather Quest forecasting competitionIn 2025, ECMWF launched the AI Weather Quest, an international competition to benchmark and improve the state of operational subseasonal forecasting18. Each week, contestants submit real-time probabilistic forecasts for weather around the globe and, at the end of each season, models with the highest skills for week 3 and week 4 are recognized as winners. To benchmark the real-time operational utility of PBC, we entered an ensemble of PBC-ECMWF and PBC-POET into the competition under the name MicroDuet. In the inaugural September–October–November season, MicroDuet did the best for all weather variables and lead times, outperforming the debiased dynamical forecasts of six operational forecasting centres (ECMWF, NOAA, ECCC, HMCR, KMA and JMA)40, a multimodel ensemble of these six dynamical forecasts, three versions of AIFS-SUBS and the forecasting systems of 34 teams worldwide (Fig. 4). MicroDuet was also the top-performing model in both forecast periods over the entire year.Fig. 4: AI Weather Quest real-time global forecast skill.Full size imageMicroDuet, an ensemble of PBC-ECMWF and PBC-POET, did best in the 2025 September–October–November AI Weather Quest competition for every variable and lead time, outperforming the debiased dynamical models of six government agencies (ECMWF, NOAA, ECCC, HMCR, KMA and JMA), their dynamical multimodel ensemble (Dynamical MME), three ECMWF AI models (including their top-performing AIFShera model) and the forecasting systems of 34 teams worldwide (including the top competitors, FengshunHybrid and LPM).Source dataThe MicroDuet skill gains are especially pronounced for precipitation, as the debiased models of all six operational forecasting centres exhibit negative skill, performing worse than the climatological average. The Dynamical MME recovers positive skill by aggregating across all six forecasting centres, but, with skills of 0.06–0.07, MicroDuet alone is twice as skilful in week 3 and thrice as skilful in week 4. MicroDuet also did best for both lead times in the December–January–February season of the Quest and, across 37 teams, was the only model to outperform Dynamical MME for all variables41. Across both seasons, MicroDuet was also recognized as the only submission to significantly outperform debiased ECMWF (P < 0.05) for all variables and lead times42.In November 2025, the week-4 temperature forecast in MicroDuet of a mid-December cold air outbreak in the Eastern USA was shared in real-time43 and verified as an extreme cold event44 that was missed by debiased ECMWF (Extended Data Fig. 8). This demonstrates the potential of PBC to improve not only general forecast quality but also the early detection of impactful extreme-weather events. We next assess the skill of PBC when trained to target such extreme events.Forecasting extreme eventsThe early identification of extreme weather is an important application of subseasonal forecasting that supports improved preparedness for hazards such as floods, heatwaves, droughts, storms and cold snaps. Figure 5 summarizes the substantial gains in extreme forecasting skill when PBC is applied to the dynamical ensemble from ECMWF. Following previous work45, we define extreme highs as events verifying above the 95th percentile and extreme lows as events verifying below the 5th percentile. We then train PBC to target semidecile (5% quantile) increments rather than quintiles and measure skill using the Brier skill score (BSS)28, a standard measure of improvement compared with a climatological baseline for a binary event.Fig. 5: Forecasting extreme weather with ECMWF and itscorrection.Full size imagea,b, Across the globe and the years 2016–2024, PBC boosts ECMWF week-3 extreme forecast skill more effectively than operational debiasing with 96% of grid cells showing skill gains for precipitation, 89% for sea-level pressure and 85% for temperature. Arid grid cells with no climatological precipitation are excluded. c, Across all 2016–2026 flood events catalogued by GDACS and severe GDACS floods with more than 100 deaths or 80,000 individuals displaced, operational debiasing routinely reduces raw ECMWF flood forecast skill, whereas PBC delivers pronounced improvements. Cross-hatching indicates significant improvement (a, paired one-sided stationary block bootstrap P < 0.05 for 939 target dates; c, paired one-sided bootstrap P < 0.05 for 88 severe and 2,435 total flood events) compared with raw and debiased ECMWF. Coastlines in b from Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com/).Source dataFor each target variable and extreme, Fig. 5a reports week-3 global BSS over the years 2016–2024, whereas Fig. 5b shows the spatial BSS distribution over the same time period. For extreme precipitation and all extreme lows, PBC again transforms its low- and no-skill inputs into skilful outputs that consistently outperform climatology. For extreme highs, PBC boosts the forecasting skill of operationally debiased ECMWF by 51% (compared with a baseline skill of 0.07) for temperature and 39% (compared with a baseline skill of 0.05) for pressure (Fig. 5a). The PBC improvements compared with debiased ECMWF are also broadly distributed with 96% of grid cells showing skill gains for precipitation, 89% for sea-level pressure and 85% for temperature (Fig. 5b). Comparable improvements are also observed in week 4 (Extended Data Fig. 9).To evaluate whether these gains translate into improved hazard prediction, Fig. 5c shows flood forecasting skill across all flood events catalogued by the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System (GDACS)46 in the years 2016–2026. For each event, flood forecasting skill is quantified by the BSS for the top precipitation semidecile across the 20° × 20° bounding box centred on the flood centroid. Given the same raw ECMWF forecasts as input, PBC boosts flood forecast skill by 76–92%, whereas debiased ECMWF dramatically reduces it, driving 0.04–0.06 baseline skills to near zero. GDACS additionally categorizes each flood on the basis of its humanitarian impact and labels a flood severe (orange or red) if it results in more than 100 deaths or 80,000 displacements46. For these high-impact events, operational debiasing only degrades or matches the 0.04–0.07 BSS of raw ECMWF, whereas PBC enhances its severe flood forecasting skill by 86–150%.DiscussionOur results indicate that probabilistic post-processing with machine learning can substantially boost the quality and usefulness of subseasonal forecasts. The PBC framework achieves this through four key properties. First, across the globe, PBC consistently improves the dynamical model from ECMWF, elevating hybrid (AI + dynamical) subseasonal forecasting. Second, PBC consistently improves leading subseasonal AI models, elevating fully data-driven subseasonal forecasting. Third, PBC forecasts are suitable for operational deployment and, in real-time competition, consistently outperform the best alternative dynamical, AI and hybrid forecasting systems worldwide. Fourth, PBC consistently improves the early detection of extreme and high-impact weather events. As climate change is predicted to increase the spatial and temporal occurrence of extreme weather, improvements in early warning capability are likely to reduce preventable morbidity and mortality19.PBC targets predictable errors rather than attempting to relearn full atmospheric dynamics. Hence, it should be viewed as an effective post-processing tool rather than a replacement for input model improvement. Fortunately, the PBC framework is also inherently adaptive: as dynamical and AI models are upgraded with improved physical representation, process representations, computational capacity or training data, PBC can be retrained to ingest and correct these higher-quality inputs. Because PBC is also inexpensive compared with the generation of large-scale dynamical or AI ensembles, the framework provides a low-overhead strategy for meteorological centres, including those in resource-constrained settings, to improve their existing forecast products.With its subseasonal lead times, PBC also targets a critical gap in the weather forecasting spectrum: at longer leads, many high-impact events are not yet predictable, whereas, at shorter leads, many warnings are no longer actionable. For example, long-lead seasonal forecasts failed to predict the disastrous 2018 Kenyan floods, but subseasonal rainfall forecasts provided a clear warning so that preparation was still possible47. Growing body of evidence demonstrates the value of skilful subseasonal forecasts for disaster response, energy production, healthcare and agriculture1,2,3, especially in semi-arid regions in Eastern and Southern Africa, where agriculture remains highly susceptible to out-of-season rains48,49. However, this evidence often takes the form of isolated case studies leveraging custom post-processing to extract signal from raw model outputs50. PBC represents an important advance for subseasonal forecasting as its low-cost skill gains generalize across target variables, input models and regions. Through the accompanying release of our open-source code, we aim to provide a standardized tool for the community to bridge the gap between raw forecasts and actionable intelligence at subseasonal horizons and beyond.MethodsProbabilistic subseasonal forecastingWe begin with a formal description of the probabilistic subseasonal forecasting problem, following the conventions of the ECMWF 2025 AI Weather Quest competition18. For each week-long period beginning on a date t, let \({{\bf{y}}}_{t}\in {{\mathbb{R}}}^{G}\) represent a vector of ground-truth weather measurements yt,g for each grid cell g in a global latitude–longitude grid. We used 1979–2026 ERA5 global reanalysis30 regridded to 1.5° × 1.5° latitude–longitude resolution as our measure of ground truth and focus on predicting average 2-m temperature, total precipitation and average mean sea-level pressure across each week-long period. Both temperature and precipitation are evaluated only over land-dominated regions (that is, grid cells with at least 50% land coverage).For each grid cell g, our aim is to predict a distribution over weather at time t, expressed as a CDF Ft,g over K = 5 historical climatological quantile bins. To this end, we set qt,g(K) = ∞ and, for each k < K, define the kth climatological quintile qt,g(k) for (t,g) as the \(\frac{k}{K}\)th quantile of the observations ys,g falling 0 days, 2 days or 4 days away from the target month–day combination in each of the previous 20 years. For each k, the probabilistic forecast Ft,g(k) represents the predicted probability that the measurement yt,g will fall below the kth quintile threshold qt,g(k).Given a test set \({{\mathcal{T}}}^{\star }\) of target dates, we measure the global quality of these probabilistic forecasts by means of the RPSS28, $$\begin{array}{c}{\rm{R}}{\rm{P}}{\rm{S}}{\rm{S}}=1-\frac{\sum _{t\in {{\mathcal{T}}}^{\star }}{\sum }_{g=1}^{G}{w}_{g}\,{{\rm{R}}{\rm{P}}{\rm{S}}}_{t,g}}{\sum _{t\in {{\mathcal{T}}}^{\star }}{\sum }_{g=1}^{G}{w}_{g}\,{\overline{{\rm{R}}{\rm{P}}{\rm{S}}}}_{t,g}}\,\,\text{for}\\ {{\rm{R}}{\rm{P}}{\rm{S}}}_{t,g}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{k=1}^{K}{({F}_{t,g}(k)-{O}_{t,g}(k))}^{2}\,{\rm{a}}{\rm{n}}{\rm{d}}\\ {\bar{{\rm{R}}{\rm{P}}{\rm{S}}}}_{t,g}=\mathop{\sum }\limits_{k=1}^{K}{\left(\frac{k}{K}-{O}_{t,g}(k)\right)}^{2},\end{array}$$where \({O}_{t,g}(k)={\mathbb{I}}[{y}_{t,g} < {q}_{t,g}(k)]\) is the observed indicator of whether yt,g falls below the kth quintile threshold, \({w}_{g}=\cos ({\rm{latitude}}(g))\) adjusts for the relative size of each grid cell, RPSt,g is termed the ranked probability score (RPS) of the forecast and \({\overline{{\rm{RPS}}}}_{t,g}\) is the RPS of a baseline climatological forecast that assigns equal probability to each quintile bin. For precipitation, arid grid cells g with no climatological precipitation (that is, with qt,g(K − 1) = 0) are excluded from this evaluation.Similarly, for a given grid cell g, we measure forecast quality over a test set \({{\mathcal{T}}}^{\star }\) by means of the spatial RPSS $${\text{Spatial RPSS}}_{g}=1-\frac{{\sum }_{t\in {{\mathcal{T}}}^{\star }}{\text{RPS}}_{t,g}}{{\sum }_{t\in {{\mathcal{T}}}^{\star }}{\overline{\text{RPS}}}_{t,g}}.$$Throughout, we evaluate RPSS at two subseasonal forecasting horizons, days 19–25 (week 3) and days 26–32 (week 4). Unless otherwise noted, we use all non-leap-day Monday and Friday target dates in the years 2016–2024 as our default test set.BaselinesExtended Data Table 1 provides a summary of the dynamical, AI, hybrid (dynamical + AI) and post-processing baselines compared with PBC in this work. Here we detail the processing steps taken to evaluate each baseline.Raw ECMWFAt each subseasonal lead time ℓ, the operational dynamical model of ECMWF17 outputs an ensemble of deterministic forecasts, \({({\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g})}_{m=1}^{M}\), each representing a possible future weather state. For each target weather variable and subseasonal horizon, we downloaded all weekly-aggregated ECMWF ensemble forecasts, spanning the years 2015–2026, from the subseasonal to seasonal (S2S) prediction project database54 through the International Research Institute for Climate and Society Data Library (IRIDL)51. Forecasts with M = 51 members (1 control and 50 perturbed) were issued every Monday and Thursday from 14 May 2015 to 26 June 2023 and forecasts with M = 101 members were issued daily starting on 28 June 2023. We converted each ensemble into a CDF forecast \({F}_{{\ell },t,g}(k)=\frac{1}{M}{\sum }_{m=1}^{M}{\mathbb{I}}[{\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g} < {q}_{t,g}(k)]\) using the climatological quintile thresholds qt,g.Debiased ECMWFTo form the debiased ECMWF baseline, we followed the operational post-processing protocol of ECMWF33 for each weather variable and subseasonal horizon. First, we downloaded all weekly-aggregated ECMWF ensemble hindcasts from the S2S database52 through the IRIDL51. Each ensemble hindcast consists of M = 11 members, \({({\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },\delta ,t,g})}_{m=1}^{M}\), indexed by a forecast target date t and the number of years δ ∈ {1, …, 20} between the forecast and corresponding hindcast target dates. Next, for each forecast target date t, we identified the set \({{\mathcal{S}}}_{t}\) of model climatology dates: the closest date no later than t with available hindcasts along with the next four and previous four available dates. We then formed model-based quintile thresholds for each forecast target date t, lead time ℓ and grid cell g by setting \({q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{ECMWF}}}(K)=\infty \) and, for each k < K, defining the kth model quintile \({q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{ecmwf}}}(k)\) as the \(\frac{k}{K}\)th quantile of all hindcasts \({\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },\delta ,s,g}\) with \(s\in {{\mathcal{S}}}_{t}\). Finally, we constructed the debiased ECMWF CDF forecast \({F}_{{\ell },t,g}(k)=\frac{1}{M}{\sum }_{m=1}^{M}{\mathbb{I}}[{\hat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g} < {q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{ECMWF}}}(k)]\).FuXi-S2SFor each target weather variable and subseasonal horizon, we downloaded 51-member ensemble forecasts, spanning the test years 2017–2021, and 51-member ensemble hindcasts, spanning the training years 2002–2016, from the official FuXi-S2S forecast dataset53. Forecasts were subsequently aggregated to a weekly resolution, with precipitation accumulated and temperature and mean sea-level pressure averaged. Following ref. 13, we form model-based quintile thresholds for each forecast target date t, lead time ℓ and grid cell g by setting \({q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{FuXi}}\,}(K)=\infty \) and, for each k < K, defining the kth model quintile \({q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{FuXi}}\,}(k)\) as the \(\frac{k}{K}\)th quantile of all hindcasts matching the target month–day combination. Finally, we constructed the CDF forecast \({F}_{{\ell },t,g}(k)=\frac{1}{M}{\sum }_{m=1}^{M}{\mathbb{I}}[{\hat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g} < {q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{FuXi}}\,}(k)]\) from each FuXi-S2S ensemble forecast \({({\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g})}_{m=1}^{M}\) with M = 51.Because FuXi-S2S and ECMWF historically issued their forecasts on different schedules, we evaluated all available forecasts from FuXi-S2S and PBC-ECMWF with target dates in the period 2017–2021. This corresponds to all Monday and Friday target dates for PBC-ECMWF and, for FuXi-S2S, all Tuesday and Friday target dates in 2017, all Wednesday and Saturday target dates in 2018, all Thursday and Sunday target dates in 2019, all Monday and Friday target dates from 3 January 2020 to 24 February 2020, all Tuesday and Saturday target dates from 29 February 2020 to 29 December 2020 and all Wednesday and Sunday target dates from 3 January 2021 to 26 December 2021.AIFS-SUBSFor each target weather variable, subseasonal horizon and odd issuance date in 2025 (except for the 31st of any month), we generated weekly-aggregated 100-member ensemble forecasts using the AIFS-SUBS model16. AIFS-SUBS follows the architecture introduced in ref. 54, combining a transformer-based graph neural network encoder and decoder with a sliding-window transformer processor in which attention is computed along spiral longitudinal bands. Ensemble members are generated by conditioning the processor on independently sampled noise, injected by means of conditional layer normalization in each processor layer and the model is trained with the fair continuous RPS loss computed over four ensemble members against ERA5 targets55. AIFS-SUBS takes two consecutive states (t − 24 h, t) as input and predicts the atmospheric state at t + 24 h. Inputs and outputs are represented on the reduced Gaussian o96 grid (approximately 1° resolution). The variant of AIFS-SUBS used in this work includes a representation of the stratosphere and was trained exclusively on ERA5 over the periods 1979–2006 and 2012–2024, leaving a 5-year validation period.Following ref. 16, for each forecast target date t, lead time ℓ and grid cell g, we generated 10-member ensemble hindcasts for the corresponding month–day combination in each of the previous 20 years, set \({q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{AIFS}}\,}(K)=\infty \) and, for each k < K, defined the kth model quintile \({q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{AIFS}}\,}(k)\) as the \(\frac{k}{K}\)th quantile of the aforementioned hindcasts. Finally, we constructed the CDF forecast \({F}_{{\ell },t,g}(k)=\frac{1}{M}{\sum }_{m=1}^{M}{\mathbb{I}}[{\hat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g} < {q}_{{\ell },t,g}^{{\rm{AIFS}}\,}(k)]\) from each AIFS ensemble forecast \({({\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g})}_{m=1}^{M}\) with M = 100.POETThe POET method29 is a member-by-member post-processing technique that has been shown to significantly improve the medium-range weather forecasting skill of ECMWF dynamical forecasts and to outperform other statistical and AI-based post-processing techniques, including the member-by-member model output statistics post-processing technique34 used operationally at the Royal Meteorological Institute of Belgium35, ensemble model output statistics36, LeNet neural network post-processing37 and pure transformer-based post-processing38. POET includes a self-attention mechanism across the ensemble member dimension in its encoder-decoder convolutional U-Net architecture, allowing the model to use context from the full input forecast distribution to minimize probabilistic forecasting error. We extended POET to subseasonal horizons by making a few minor modifications to its data-processing pipeline and architecture.First, we applied POET to weekly aggregates of weather variables rather than the instantaneous values appropriate for medium-range forecasting. As input features, we used all available variables from the S2S database52 and a collection of 36 constant fields from ERA530, including orography, a land–sea mask and soil and vegetation types. Following common practice for feature embeddings, metadata, including the constant fields, lead time and weekly-averaged top-of-atmosphere incoming solar radiation, were embedded with a learned convolutional layer and used to update the highest-level features additively. To accommodate the larger set of input and output features, the model size was increased to approximately 27 million trainable parameters by increasing the number of latent features and the number of ensemble transformer layers.POET is configured by default to predict several targets, including geopotential heights, wind and humidity on a few pressure levels and surface winds and humidity, in addition to the target variables temperature, mean sea-level pressure and precipitation. Although predicting several targets improves consistency between variables, we found that the single-target model produced higher-quality outputs for precipitation on our validation set. Hence, the final results reported for POET are from the multi-target model for temperature and pressure and from the single-target model for precipitation. The POET models were developed using the 20 years of 10-member ECMWF hindcasts issued in 2024, with the hindcasts for the years 2004–2022 used for training and the 2023 hindcasts used for validation.For each target weather variable, subseasonal horizon and ECMWF forecast issuance date in 2024 (every Monday and Thursday to 21 November and every odd date thereafter), we generated weekly-aggregated ensemble forecasts, \({({\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g})}_{m=1}^{M}\), by applying POET to the M = 100 perturbed ECMWF ensemble members. We then converted each ensemble into a CDF forecast \({F}_{{\ell },t,g}(k)=\frac{1}{M}{\sum }_{m=1}^{M}{\mathbb{I}}[{\widehat{y}}_{m,{\ell },t,g} < {q}_{t,g}(k)]\) using the climatological quintile thresholds qt,g.PBCPBC (Fig. 1) corrects the systematic errors in probabilistic forecasts by training and applying two complementary machine learning corrections (Debias++ and Persistence++), projecting the output of each onto the space of valid distributions and finally averaging the resulting distributions. For a given weather variable, target date t⋆ and lead time ℓ⋆, each machine learning algorithm is given access to a model’s uncorrected CDF forecasts \({{\bf{F}}}_{{{\ell }}^{\star },{t}^{\star }}={({F}_{{{\ell }}^{\star },{t}^{\star },g})}_{g=1}^{G}\) for the target, a dataset of historical CDF forecasts \({{\bf{F}}}_{{\ell },t}={({F}_{{\ell },t,g})}_{g=1}^{G}\) from the model with training set target dates \(t\in {\mathcal{T}}\) and lead times \({\ell }\in {\mathcal{L}}\) and observed cumulative quantile bin indicators \({{\bf{O}}}_{t}={({O}_{t,g})}_{g=1}^{G}\) for each \(t\in {\mathcal{T}}\). To mimic operational deployment, each algorithm is only given access to training observations that would have been fully observable ℓ⋆ − 1 days previous to the target date t⋆.Debias++
                        For each quantile bin k, Debias++ (Algorithm 1) performs probabilistic forecast correction in four steps. First, to account for heterogeneity in forecast errors over time, Debias++ adaptively selects a span s of observations around the target day of year for probabilistic debiasing and a range d⋆ of forecast issuance dates for ensembling. Second, Debias++ forms ensemble mean probabilistic forecasts \({\overline{{\bf{F}}}}_{t}(k)\) by averaging its input CDF forecasts over the selected range of issuance dates. Third, to directly counteract systematic errors, Debias++ corrects the target CDF forecast \({\overline{{\bf{F}}}}_{{t}^{\star }}(k)\) by subtracting the probabilistic prediction bias—the average forecast value \({\overline{{\bf{F}}}}_{t}(k)\) minus the average observed value Ot(k)—over the selected debiasing window across the previous Y years.                 Projection and ensemblingIt is possible for the quantile bin predictions of Debias++ and Persistence++ to violate the constraint that cumulative probabilities must be non-decreasing across quantile thresholds. In such cases, we use isotonic regression56 to project their output forecasts onto the space of valid CDFs. This operation is guaranteed to improve forecast skill as, by minimizing squared error to the set of valid CDFs, it increases RPSS for all possible observations simultaneously. The final PBC forecast averages the two projected corrections to capture the complementary benefits of each.MicroDuetTo form the MicroDuet model used in the AI Weather Quest, we considered three combinations of the PBC-ECMWF and PBC-POET forecasts—an equal-weighted average, full weight on PBC-ECMWF and full weight on PBC-POET—and selected the combination that maximized 2024 RPSS for each variable and lead time. Data availability
            
            All ERA5 data used in this study is available through the Climate Data Store of the Copernicus Climate Change Service (https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu). All dynamical data used in this study are available in the S2S prediction project database52. S2S is a joint initiative of the World Weather Research Programme and the World Climate Research Programme. The original S2S database is hosted at ECMWF as an extension of the TIGGE database (https://apps.ecmwf.int/datasets/data/s2s). All AI Weather Quest evaluations are available through the AI Weather Quest leaderboard (https://aiweatherquest.ecmwf.int/leaderboards/). All FuXi-S2S forecasts are available in the official FuXi-S2S forecast dataset53. All flood events are available through the GDACS REST API (https://www.gdacs.org). All maps were generated using the Cartopy Python package61 with coastlines, continguous US borders and lake boundaries provided by Natural Earth (https://www.naturalearthdata.com/). Source data are provided with this paper.

items.title: Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity
items.body:
EDITORIAL
                    
                        14 October 2026

Protecting nature means valuing biodiversity

Appeals for extra money are failing. Fundamental changes are needed to safeguard the planet for future generations.

Joni Mitchell performed her environmental anthem Big Yellow Taxi at the 1970 Isle of Wight Festival, which attracted around 600,000 people.Credit: Tony Russell/Redferns/GettyThe words of Canadian-American singer-songwriter Joni Mitchell’s 1970 environmental anthem Big Yellow Taxi will be echoing in the halls of the United Nations biodiversity conference (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, that begins on 19 October.Don’t it always seem to go / That you don’t know what you’ve got / Till it’s gone / They paved paradise / And put up a parking lot.“Nature is in freefall,” according to the Living Planet Report 2026, published on 7 October by conservation charity WWF. Between 1970 and 2022, the sizes of vertebrate wildlife populations that WWF research teams have been monitoring decreased by 73% (see go.nature.com/4zy2zxd).Lay of the land: terrestrial conservation efforts cover a wider area than thoughtAlmost four years ago at COP15 in Montreal, Canada, countries agreed on targets to stop and eventually reverse biodiversity loss by 2050. The goals included protecting 30% of land and water habitats by 2030 (also called the 30 × 30 target) and to substantially increase annual funding for conservation from public and private sources — to at least US$30 billion for low-income nations and small island states — by the end of the decade. Although these goals are not currently on course to be met, official figures could be underestimating the global amount of protected land, suggests a study published on 14 October (H. M. K. O’Neill et al. Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11157-4; 2026).The Living Planet Report notes that some species are no longer considered endangered — including the Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) and the green sea turtle (Chelonia mydas). But if the global decline in biodiversity is to be halted, a much more fundamental change is needed: the value of natural capital and ecosystem services must be factored into nations’ decision-making.Many of the poorest countries that are rich in biodiversity rely heavily on international public and philanthropic funding to protect their natural resources. In Montreal, countries promised to mobilize at least $200 billion per year by the end of the decade. Some estimates suggest that the world has already surpassed that: global biodiversity finance trebled from roughly $100 billion in 2019 to around $300 billion in 2024, according to reports by the Paulson Institute, a think tank in Chicago, Illinois (see go.nature.com/3vuuvfz and go.nature.com/4yhgtuc). As of June 2025, 12 national and regional governments have contributed $386 million to a biodiversity fund for low- and middle-income countries. The fund currently supports 82 projects, including initiatives backing ecotourism in Indonesia and locally managed marine conservation in Madagascar.The problem is that spending on activities that harm nature strongly exceeds the boost to biodiversity finance. For instance, it will now cost around $1.3 trillion a year to achieve the 30 × 30 target by 2030, suggests the Paulson Institute report. Moreover, several small but important biodiversity funds are struggling. For instance, the Cali Fund, which was launched last year, has received barely any donations so far. Companies that profit from using genetic-sequence data gathered in biodiversity-rich nations are encouraged to pay into this pot. As of now, businesses have contributed a grand total of $6,000.Biodiversity conservation has an evidence problem — it’s time to fix itSome economists say that to save nature, the world can’t rely on public funding or voluntary contributions from businesses. Government aid to low- and middle-income countries dropped last year by 23% compared with 2024, according to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. Researchers are instead proposing that countries cut public subsidies that harm nature and that they end or reform environment-damaging policies.In its State of Finance for Nature 2026 report, the UN Environment Programme estimates that public spending on fossil-fuel subsidies exceeded $1 trillion in 2023 (see go.nature.com/3trvr2y). As well as harming nature, such subsidies can be counterproductive, too. Many governments, for instance, pay farmers to use pesticides that reduce the biodiversity needed for agriculture to be productive.But cutting subsidies and even reforming them is difficult. Governments use subsidies to support businesses and protect jobs. Financial aid, including for energy and food, is also used to keep prices down for households when the cost of living is increasing.China and many European countries are making progress by tying farm subsidies to environmental objectives, such as improved soil health, or by paying farmers to plant hedges and wildflowers. But these initiatives are in their early stages, and implementation is patchy.Don’t rush rules for sharing digital genetic-sequence informationIf aid is faltering and redirected subsidies won’t bridge the biodiversity-funding gap, something else needs to happen. Researchers argue that the people who run their nation’s economy — the ministers of finance and their teams — should be factoring the true costs of nature into their decision-making.If, for example, a local or national government plans to convert part of a wetland for industrial use, any projections of economic benefits should be compared with the services provided by wetlands that will be lost, such as wildlife habitats, water purification and carbon sequestration. If bee populations decline because of habitat loss, their pollination services — crucial to human survival — will be lost. However, the cost of replacing such services is rarely factored in when land is converted.For some years, China’s decision makers, together with the Natural Capital Alliance, a multidisciplinary team of researchers in China, Europe and the United States, have been studying how to incorporate such analyses into the country’s economic and industrial policies, using a concept called gross ecosystem product. Such an approach needs to be adopted by policymakers in other countries, too.As long as countries regard ecosystems as being cost-free, they will always need appeals to altruism to protect nature — appeals that are increasingly failing. It’s encouraging that finance ministers are expected to join their environmental counterparts at COP17. Achieving the Herculean task of protecting ecosystems and biodiversity requires the world to change how it values nature.Mitchell’s words should not become a self-fulfilling prophecy: make sure we protect nature, because “you don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone”.

E’ tornata libera la cicogna salvata dai volontari WWF in Campania
items.description:
La cicogna era stata inanellata in Polonia lo scorso 16 giugno: si trattava di un giovane al suo primo volo di migrazione.
The post E’ tornata l
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie I primi a intervenire i volontari del WWF “Terre del Tirreno” Dopo una degenza di un paio di settimane al Cras il Frullone di Napoli è tornata libera la cicogna bianca recuperata in località Marina del Cantone nel Comune di Massa Lubrense.L’animale era stato avvistato da alcuni giorni su di una terrazza di un albergo sul mare e sembrava non avere alcuna ferita apparente. Appena allertati della presenza di una cicogna “inanellata” i volontari del WWF Terre del Tirreno, col presidente Claudio d’Esposito e il biologo Fabio Russo, si sono subito recati sul posto. La cicogna appariva debilitata e si faceva avvicinare e prendere senza alcuna resistenza. Dal becco di un colore non rosso acceso e ancora col nero in punta si deduceva che fosse un esemplare giovane. La cicogna era stata inanellata in Polonia Dall’analisi dei dati contenuti negli anelli sulle zampe si è potuto risalire alla sua storia: la cicogna era stata inanellata in Polonia il 16 giugno 2026 e si trattava di un pullus al suo primo volo di migrazione. Il Responsabile dell’ASL veterinaria di Piano di Sorrento allertava quindi con urgenza l’ambulanza che provvedeva a trasferire l’animale al Centro Recupero Fauna Selvatica il Frullone di Napoli.I veterinari del CRAS hanno in seguito accertato una situazione di debilitazione con problematiche di tipo metabolico. Dopo un periodo di cure la giovane cicogna è stata inserita nelle voliere di riabilitazione fino alla sua completa ripresa. Quindi si è provveduto al rilascio in un’idonea località nell’avellinese, per permettergli di continuare a nutrirsi in natura e riprendere il suo viaggio di migrazione verso sud all’arrivo dell’inverno. Senza l’intervento del WWF non ce l’avrebbe fatta “Siamo contenti del lieto fine di questa storia – dichiara Claudio d’Esposito presidente del WWF Terre del Tirreno – vedere una cicogna è considerato da sempre un presagio positivo, simbolo universale di buona fortuna, prosperità e arrivo di buone notizie. La giovane cicogna senza l’intervento umano stavolta non ce l’avrebbe fatta. La cicogna in natura può vivere 30 anni, il record per una cicogna selvatica è di 39 anni, se supera le difficoltà dei primi anni di vita. La mortalità di tale specie infatti è alta durante i primi due anni e soprattutto durante i lunghi viaggi di migrazione verso l’Africa, a causa di una serie di pericoli come cavi elettrici, scarsità di cibo o il bracconaggio.Grazie agli anelli sulle zampe abbiamo potuto acquisire una serie di importanti dati sull’animale e sulla rotta del viaggio. Gli anelli leggeri, di metallo o plastica, sono posti sulla zampa dell’uccello da ornitologi esperti e ogni anello ha un numero unico e il nome dell’istituto di ricerca. Una sorta di carta d’identità: quando un uccello viene trovato o ricatturato dalla lettura del codice si scopre la sua storia”.

items.description:
Le grandi migrazioni ci insegnano che tutto è connesso, anche a migliaia di km. di distanza
The post Il 10 ottobre è la Giornata Mondiale degli uccell
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie Le aree umide al centro delle rotte migratorie Dalle riserve naturali e Oasi WWF delle Saline di Trapani e Valpredina, nelle prealpi bergamasche, due storie sorprendenti che ci raccontano i grandi viaggi dei migratori alati e l’importanza di tutelare le rotte migratorie dalla caccia (e bracconaggio) e attraverso la tutela delle aree di sosta e svernamento: tra tutti, le aree umide. La storia del biancone che sembrava spacciato Il 31 luglio 2025, il C.R.A.S. WWF di Valpredina riceve un biancone (Circaetus gallicus), proveniente da Sedrina, in Val Brembana (BG). Alla prima visita, le condizioni dell’animale appaiono subito serie: presenta una profonda lesione lacero-contusa, una frattura del radio sinistro. Il rapace è fortemente debilitato. Gli esami radiografici evidenziano la presenza di frammenti di piombo, compatibili con il probabile passaggio di un pallino da caccia. Inizia così un lungo percorso di cure e riabilitazione. Lo staff veterinario esegue due interventi chirurgici per rimuovere i tessuti necrotici e ricostruire la parte cutanea danneggiata.Rimangono, però, forti sospetti di lesioni a carico dei tendini e l’animale viene sottoposto a diversi trattamenti farmacologici per contrastare il rischio di infezioni. Dopo circa tre mesi di cure, il biancone continua a non utilizzare correttamente l’ala e la sua capacità di volo appare compromessa. Dopo altri due mesi, in assenza di miglioramenti significativi, si decide quindi di trasferirlo in una voliera destinata agli animali non più recuperabili. La storia, però, non è ancora finita. Nella primavera del 2026 la sorpresa Il biancone in cura al CRAS WWF Valpredina gli operatori osservano un inatteso e importante miglioramento della mobilità dell’ala. Il rapace viene trasferito in una voliera più grande, per verificare le sue reali capacità di volo. La sorpresa è straordinaria: il biancone ricomincia a volare correttamente, senza evidenti deficit. Nel giro di pochi mesi recupera anche una buona tonicità muscolare.Si decide così di programmarne la liberazione, non prima di aver acquistato un dispositivo GPS per seguirne gli spostamenti. Dopo l’inanellamento da parte di ISPRA, che permette di stabilire che si tratta di un maschio adulto, arriva finalmente il momento tanto atteso. Nel luglio 2026, dopo 344 giorni di degenza, il biancone viene restituito alla natura. Il GPS racconta così una nuova pagina della sua storia: dopo alcuni giorni trascorsi nella media Val Seriana, il 29 agosto inizia una lunga migrazione verso sud-ovest. Attraversa la pianura padana, le Alpi occidentali, la Francia, supera i Pirenei e, il 9 settembre alle 16:00, affronta lo stretto di Gibilterra, raggiungendo l’Africa in appena 30 minuti. Il percorso prosegue quindi dritto verso sud e, il 20 settembre, il biancone è ormai in Mali, dove cambia direzione e si sposta verso est, esplorando il territorio fino a raggiungere le sponde del fiume Niger, dove si trova attualmente. Ma la storia continua… La storia di Icaro Nella Riserva Naturale Regionale “Saline di Trapani e Paceco”, gestita dal WWF Italia, tra le migliaia di uccelli che ogni anno arrivano, partono, sostano o trascorrono l’inverno, ce n’è una che ormai conosciamo quasi per nome. La sigla è ICLK, il nome che gli è stato affibbiato è Icaro. È una spatola (Platalea leucorodia), riconoscibile grazie alla sigla riportata sull’anello colorato che porta alla zampa, osservata e fotografata lo scorso 22 settembre dall’ornitologo Andrea Cusmano. Una storia lunga 18 anni La spatola Icaro- G. Cusimano Icaro è stato inanellato il 16 aprile 2008 a Valle Mandriole, nel Ravennate, all’interno del sistema delle zone umide del Delta del Po. Nel febbraio 2011 viene osservata per la prima volta nella Riserva delle Saline di Trapani e Paceco, a centinaia di chilometri dal luogo in cui era nata. Ma è la sequenza degli avvistamenti successivi a rendere particolarmente significativa la sua storia: nel settembre 2011 Icaro viene nuovamente osservato nel ravennate e appena due mesi dopo, nel novembre dello stesso anno, è di nuovo alle Saline di Paceco.Una successione di spostamenti che rende visibile, attraverso la storia di un singolo individuo, il collegamento ecologico tra le zone umide del Delta del Po e quelle della Sicilia occidentale. Oggi, diciotto anni dopo la nascita, Icaro continua a tornare alle Saline di Trapani. La nuova osservazione del settembre 2026 aggiunge un altro importante tassello alla sua storia di vita e conferma il legame di questo individuo con le zone umide del trapanese, uno dei luoghi che evidentemente fanno parte della geografia della sua vita. La conservazione non può farsi a compartimenti stagni Icaro ci mostra concretamente come gli uccelli migratori non conoscano confini amministrativi e come la loro conservazione dipenda dall’esistenza di una rete di ambienti idonei (la Rete Natura 2000) distribuiti lungo le rotte migratorie. La biodiversità, infatti, non può essere tutelata pensando ai territori come isole separate: la conservazione richiede connessioni ecologiche, collaborazione tra aree protette, condivisione dei dati scientifici e scambio di buone pratiche. CRAS VALPREDINA Il  C.R.A.S. WWF di Valpredina è una struttura realizzata dal WWF Italia con lo scopo di curare la fauna selvatica ferita o in difficoltà per recuperarla e rimetterla in libertà; il Centro inoltre svolge una costante attività di… Scopri di più Saline di Trapani Le saline di Trapani e Paceco rappresentano uno scampolo di Natura sottratta 26 anni fa all’espansione urbana grazie all’istituzione della Riserva; oltre ad essere tra le ultime saline rimaste produttive in Sicilia sono anche uno scrigno di biodiversità,… Scopri di più

items.title: Commissione Ue pubblica le linee guida Sump 2026: 431 nodi urbani europei verso piani di mobilità sostenibile entro il 2027
items.description: La Commissione europea pubblica le linee guida Sump 2026. Scopri gli obblighi vincolanti per i piani di mobilità sostenibile e le scadenze per le ammi
items.body:
Mobilità

Commissione Ue pubblica le linee guida Sump 2026: 431 nodi urbani europei verso piani di mobilità sostenibile entro il 2027

Roberto Torcolacci

-

8 Ottobre 2026

L’8 giugno 2026 l’EU Urban Mobility Observatory ha pubblicato la terza edizione delle linee guida europee per lo sviluppo e l’implementazione dei Sustainable Urban Mobility Plans (SUMP), segnando un passaggio concreto verso l’obbligo — non più una raccomandazione — per centinaia di città europee di dotarsi di piani di mobilità sostenibile entro una scadenza precisa. Il documento è stato realizzato nell’ambito del contratto di servizio con la Direzione Generale per la Mobilità e i Trasporti della Commissione europea (DG MOVE), e arriva in un momento in cui le politiche di trasporto urbano stanno diventando uno degli assi portanti della transizione ecologica continentale.
Un obbligo per 431 nodi urbani europei
Il dato più rilevante delle nuove linee guida non riguarda la metodologia, ma la portata regolatoria che le accompagna. Il Regolamento TEN-T rivisto impone a 431 nodi urbani distribuiti in tutta Europa di adottare un piano urbano di mobilità sostenibile entro la fine del 2027. Non si tratta di un invito o di un incentivo: è un requisito vincolante, che trasforma i SUMP da strumento volontario a obbligo di pianificazione per un numero significativo di amministrazioni locali.
Questo cambiamento di natura — da raccomandazione a prescrizione — rappresenta una discontinuità rispetto alle edizioni precedenti delle linee guida. Le città coinvolte fanno parte della rete transeuropea dei trasporti e la loro adesione ai piani di mobilità sostenibile è ora condizione necessaria per l’integrazione coerente di quella rete. Il termine del 2027 lascia poco più di un anno alle amministrazioni che non hanno ancora avviato il processo per completarlo.
Cosa cambia rispetto alle edizioni precedenti
La terza edizione mantiene la struttura del ciclo di pianificazione consolidata nelle versioni precedenti, ma integra gli sviluppi normativi più recenti adottati a livello europeo. Le nuove linee guida sono allineate con un insieme di quadri regolatori e strategici che negli ultimi anni hanno ridisegnato le priorità della mobilità urbana nel contesto comunitario:Leggi ancheMinistero delle Infrastrutture e della Mobilità Sostenibili, cosa cambiaArea C Milano, si riparte da oggi: orario ed esenzioni
👉 Leggi anche: Mobilità urbana sostenibile: la Commissione Ue pubblica le nuove linee guida Sump 2026

il Green Deal europeo, che fissa obiettivi di riduzione delle emissioni di gas serra;
la Strategia per una mobilità sostenibile e intelligente, che punta a rendere il sistema dei trasporti europeo più efficiente e a basse emissioni;
il Quadro politico per la sicurezza stradale, che integra la dimensione della sicurezza nella pianificazione urbana;
il nuovo Quadro europeo per la mobilità urbana, che fornisce un riferimento aggiornato per le politiche locali.

L’allineamento con questi strumenti non è puramente formale. Significa che i piani di mobilità sostenibile adottati dai 431 nodi urbani dovranno rispondere a obiettivi misurabili che spaziano dalla riduzione delle emissioni all’aumento della sicurezza stradale, passando per l’intermodalità e l’accessibilità dei trasporti pubblici.
Perché le linee guida SUMP 2026 contano per le amministrazioni locali
Per molte amministrazioni, specialmente quelle di medie dimensioni, il recepimento di questi obblighi richiede un salto di capacità progettuale non trascurabile. Sviluppare un piano urbano di mobilità sostenibile non significa semplicemente redigere un documento: implica analisi della domanda di trasporto, coinvolgimento degli stakeholder locali, definizione di scenari alternativi, indicatori di monitoraggio e meccanismi di revisione periodica.
Immagine generata con AI
Le linee guida pubblicate dall’EU Urban Mobility Observatory servono precisamente a questo: fornire un quadro metodologico condiviso che consenta alle città di affrontare il processo in modo strutturato, indipendentemente dalla loro dimensione o dal livello di esperienza pregressa in materia di pianificazione della mobilità. Il fatto che la struttura del ciclo di pianificazione sia stata mantenuta rispetto alle edizioni precedenti è un segnale di continuità che facilita il lavoro delle amministrazioni già impegnate in processi SUMP avviati negli anni scorsi.
Il contesto: perché proprio ora
La scelta di pubblicare la terza edizione nel giugno 2026 non è casuale. Il Regolamento TEN-T rivisto è entrato in vigore con scadenze operative che si avvicinano rapidamente, e le città incluse nei 431 nodi urbani avevano bisogno di un riferimento aggiornato per orientare la propria pianificazione. Senza linee guida allineate ai nuovi quadri normativi europei, il rischio era quello di produrre piani già parzialmente obsoleti rispetto agli obblighi regolatori.
👉 Leggi anche: Italia, due mesi per presentare il piano nazionale di ristrutturazione edilizia o rischia sanzioni UE
Il contesto politico più ampio è quello di un’Unione europea che ha fatto della decarbonizzazione dei trasporti uno degli obiettivi centrali del proprio percorso verso la neutralità climatica. I trasporti urbani incidono in modo rilevante sulle emissioni totali di CO₂ nelle aree metropolitane, e i piani di mobilità sostenibile sono considerati uno degli strumenti più efficaci per intervenire su questa quota, agendo sulla composizione modale degli spostamenti — favorendo il trasporto pubblico, la mobilità attiva e la riduzione del traffico privato motorizzato.
Le linee guida complete sono disponibili attraverso l’portale ufficiale della Commissione europea dedicato ai trasporti, dove è possibile consultare anche i materiali di supporto prodotti dall’EU Urban Mobility Observatory.
Le implicazioni per l’Italia
L’Italia è tra i Paesi con nodi urbani inclusi nella rete TEN-T, il che significa che alcune delle principali città italiane rientrano nell’obbligo di adottare un SUMP entro il 2027. Per le amministrazioni italiane, questo si traduce nella necessità di allineare i propri strumenti di pianificazione — i Piani Urbani della Mobilità Sostenibile (PUMS) già previsti dalla normativa nazionale — con i requisiti aggiornati delle nuove linee guida europee.
In Italia il PUMS è già uno strumento consolidato, introdotto dal decreto legislativo n. 257 del 2016 e successivamente rafforzato nelle sue prescrizioni. Tuttavia, l’aggiornamento europeo del 2026 introduce nuovi elementi di allineamento con le strategie comunitarie che potrebbero richiedere revisioni o integrazioni rispetto ai piani già adottati o in fase di elaborazione.
La scadenza del 2027 è ravvicinata, ma non impossibile per le città che hanno già avviato percorsi strutturati. Per quelle che partono da zero, invece, il tempo disponibile richiede di muoversi con rapidità, senza rinunciare alla qualità di un processo partecipato che le stesse linee guida indicano come elemento fondante di qualsiasi piano urbano di mobilità sostenibile credibile ed efficace.

items.title: Legge Gadda 166/2016: dieci anni di risultati e impatto sulla riduzione dello spreco alimentare in Italia
items.description: La legge Gadda 166/2016 ha trasformato il contrasto allo spreco alimentare in Italia: 3,7 milioni di tonnellate donate e 10,3 miliardi di valore in di
items.body:
Sostenibilità

Legge Gadda 166/2016: dieci anni di risultati e impatto sulla riduzione dello spreco alimentare in Italia

Roberto Torcolacci

-

8 Ottobre 2026

Il 14 settembre 2016 l’Italia si dotava di una delle normative più avanzate in Europa per contrastare lo spreco alimentare: la Legge 166/2016, nota come legge Gadda. A dieci anni dall’entrata in vigore, i numeri raccontano qualcosa di concreto: circa 3,7 milioni di tonnellate di eccedenze alimentari donate e un valore complessivo di donazioni — alimentari e farmaceutiche — che supera i 10,3 miliardi di euro. Non si tratta di una semplice fotografia statistica, ma della misura di quanto una legge possa cambiare abitudini, filiere e cultura.
Cosa ha cambiato davvero la legge Gadda sullo spreco alimentare
Prima del 2016, donare eccedenze alimentari in Italia era tecnicamente possibile, ma burocraticamente scoraggiante. Le aziende della grande distribuzione, i produttori e i ristoratori si trovavano di fronte a un sistema fiscale e normativo che rendeva la cessione gratuita di cibo più complicata dello smaltimento. Il risultato era paradossale: prodotti ancora perfettamente commestibili finivano nei rifiuti mentre milioni di persone in difficoltà economica faticavano ad accedere a cibo sufficiente.
La legge Gadda ha ribaltato questa logica. Il principio fondamentale è semplice: semplificare e incentivare la donazione, rimuovendo gli ostacoli fiscali e burocratici che la rendevano poco conveniente per chi cedeva il cibo. In pratica, la legge ha introdotto una presunzione di cessione gratuita per le eccedenze donate a enti del Terzo Settore, eliminando l’obbligo di documentazione dettagliata per ogni singolo trasferimento e alleggerendo il carico IVA sulle donazioni.
Non meno importante è stata la semplificazione delle responsabilità: chi dona cibo in buona fede a un’organizzazione riconosciuta non risponde penalmente di eventuali problemi successivi alla consegna, a condizione che le merci siano state cedute nel rispetto delle norme igienico-sanitarie. Questo ha liberato molte aziende da una paura che, prima del 2016, era uno dei principali freni alla donazione.Leggi ancheCarnevale: 6 decorazioni ecologiche per la casaTransizione energetica in Italia: in vigore ad oggi il decreto sulle Comunità Energetiche Rinnovabili
I numeri di un decennio: 3,7 milioni di tonnellate e oltre 10 miliardi di valore
I dati aggregati dei dieci anni di applicazione della legge restituiscono una dimensione che va oltre le aspettative iniziali. Circa 3,7 milioni di tonnellate di eccedenze alimentari sono state recuperate e redistribuite sul territorio italiano, secondo quanto riportato da fonti istituzionali e del Terzo Settore. Se si aggiunge la componente farmaceutica — anch’essa inclusa nell’ambito applicativo della norma — il valore totale delle donazioni raggiunge i 10,3 miliardi di euro.
Per dare una misura di cosa significhino concretamente 3,7 milioni di tonnellate, si può pensare al cibo che ogni anno viene recuperato da supermercati, mense aziendali, industrie alimentari, panifici, mercati ortofrutticoli e ristoranti, e che invece di diventare rifiuto arriva a famiglie in difficoltà, mense sociali, centri di accoglienza, comunità terapeutiche. La rete che gestisce questi flussi è composta da centinaia di organizzazioni non profit distribuite su tutto il territorio nazionale, che operano come intermediari tra chi produce o vende cibo e chi ne ha bisogno.
La legge ha inoltre avuto un effetto indiretto ma rilevante: ha normalizzato culturalmente la donazione. Molte aziende che inizialmente aderivano per ragioni fiscali hanno progressivamente integrato il recupero delle eccedenze nelle proprie politiche di sostenibilità, trasformando una pratica di compliance in una scelta identitaria.
👉 Leggi anche: Italia, due mesi per presentare il piano nazionale di ristrutturazione edilizia o rischia sanzioni UE
Il ruolo del Terzo Settore come infrastruttura della redistribuzione
Immagine generata con AI
La legge Gadda non ha creato dal nulla una rete di redistribuzione: ha potenziato e legittimato quella già esistente. Organizzazioni come il Banco Alimentare e numerose realtà caritative locali — molte delle quali legate a Caritas o ad associazioni laiche — operavano già nel recupero del cibo prima del 2016. La norma ha però fornito loro un quadro giuridico stabile, ha aumentato il numero di donatori disposti a collaborare e ha reso più prevedibili i flussi di prodotto.
Il meccanismo funziona su più livelli. A livello industriale, i grandi produttori cedono lotti di prodotto con difetti estetici, confezioni danneggiate o prossimi alla scadenza. A livello della distribuzione, i supermercati attivano protocolli quotidiani di raccolta delle eccedenze fresche — pane, frutta, verdura, latticini — che vengono ritirati da volontari o corrieri dedicati. A livello della ristorazione, mense e catering possono cedere pasti confezionati non distribuiti, nel rispetto delle norme sulla catena del freddo.
Questa infrastruttura richiede però risorse: mezzi di trasporto refrigerati, magazzini, personale formato, sistemi di tracciabilità. Uno dei limiti strutturali della legge è che non prevede finanziamenti diretti alle organizzazioni intermediarie: il meccanismo incentiva la donazione da parte di chi cede il cibo, ma non copre i costi operativi di chi lo raccoglie e redistribuisce. Molte realtà del Terzo Settore fanno leva su fondi europei, contributi comunali e donazioni private per sostenere questi costi, con una variabilità territoriale significativa.
Cosa resta ancora da fare: limiti applicativi e sfide aperte
Dieci anni di applicazione hanno messo in luce alcune aree di miglioramento. La frammentazione territoriale è forse il problema più evidente: l’efficacia della legge dipende molto dalla densità e dalla capacità organizzativa del Terzo Settore locale. In alcune aree del Sud Italia, dove le reti di redistribuzione sono meno strutturate, le eccedenze vengono recuperate in misura inferiore rispetto al Nord, dove la presenza di organizzazioni come il Banco Alimentare è più capillare.
Un secondo nodo riguarda la piccola ristorazione e il commercio di prossimità. Bar, trattorie, negozi alimentari di quartiere producono eccedenze quotidiane, ma spesso non hanno le risorse né le competenze per attivare protocolli di donazione conformi alla normativa. La legge prevede semplificazioni, ma il passaggio dalla norma alla pratica richiede accompagnamento e formazione che non sempre sono disponibili.
C’è poi la questione della misurazione dell’impatto. I dati aggregati sui volumi donati esistono, ma mancano ancora sistemi omogenei di rilevazione che permettano di confrontare i risultati anno per anno e territorio per territorio in modo sistematico. Senza questa base informativa, è difficile valutare dove concentrare gli sforzi e quali leve normative o operative siano più efficaci.
Sul fronte europeo, la legge Gadda ha rappresentato un modello di riferimento nel dibattito sulla legislazione anti-spreco. Il Ministero dell’Agricoltura, della Sovranità Alimentare e delle Foreste ha continuato a monitorare l’applicazione della norma nell’ambito delle politiche nazionali per la sostenibilità alimentare, anche in raccordo con le direttive europee in materia di economia circolare.
Dopo dieci anni, la legge Gadda rimane uno strumento legislativo solido, capace di produrre risultati misurabili su scala nazionale. I 3,7 milioni di tonnellate recuperate e i 10,3 miliardi di valore redistribuito non sono numeri astratti: corrispondono a pasti serviti, a famiglie sostenute, a cibo sottratto alle discariche. La sfida dei prossimi anni sarà consolidare ciò che funziona, colmare i divari territoriali e aggiornare la norma là dove la realtà ha superato le previsioni del legislatore del 2016.
